analysis.one_liner: Raises the tax deduction for business meals and entertainment from 50% to 80% of their cost.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote, despite sponsorship by a Democratic senator and eight cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let businesses deduct 80% of the cost of client meals and entertainment from their taxable income instead of the 50% allowed at the time. That larger write-off would cut tax bills for companies that entertain clients, but reduce federal revenue. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that spend on meals and entertainment for clients and associates, which could deduct 80% instead of 50% of those costs, cutting their tax bills. High-end restaurants, event venues, and the entertainment and hospitality industry would gain customers whose visits are effectively tax-subsidized. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Businesses could deduct 80% of meal and entertainment expenses instead of 50%, directly lowering their tax bills on client entertainment spending.
The change would apply retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 1996, giving businesses a larger write-off starting with the 1997 tax year.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced federal revenue, since businesses would deduct 30 cents more per dollar of meal and entertainment spending from their taxable income. All other taxpayers either pay more or receive less to make up the difference. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces federal revenue by letting businesses write off 30 cents more per dollar of meal and entertainment spending, with the lost revenue made up by other taxpayers or lower federal spending.

The 50% limit was enacted in 1993 specifically to curb what lawmakers viewed as excessive tax-subsidized business entertaining; this bill would have reversed that restraint with no offsetting revenue.
The benefit flows to businesses in proportion to how much they spend entertaining clients, which concentrates the value among larger companies and high-spending industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a straightforward tax cut to businesses that entertain clients, and its supporters would argue it partially undoes a 1993 tax increase on business entertainment. But it does nothing to offset the lost revenue, and the benefits skew toward larger businesses and hospitality-related spending rather than ordinary wage earners. Given that it never received any committee action, its practical effect on anyone was zero.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 21, 1997, by Senator Inouye with three original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
It eventually attracted eight cosponsors, seven Republicans and one Democrat, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote in committee.
Its entire recorded history is introduction and referral; no further action appears before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that deduct business meals and entertainment are no worse off, since the deduction stayed at 50% rather than being restored to 80% — nothing changed for anyone. The tax treatment in place before the bill remains the same.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses that deduct meals and entertainment

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan but thinly supported: a Democratic sponsor with eight cosponsors, seven of them Republicans, and it never advanced.

industries.industry: Corporations and businesses that deduct client meals and entertainment
industries.note: Businesses claiming the deduction would pay less tax, shifting the cost onto other taxpayers.
Raising the deduction from 50% to 80% makes tax-subsidized client entertaining cheaper, encouraging more business at restaurants, event venues, and entertainment providers.
Entertainment spending by businesses would be 30% more deductible, increasing demand for tickets, sports seats, and events paid for with pre-tax dollars.
